dmm-2010-power-01.prompt:
We denote the probability of event $A$ happening as $P(A)$. The conditional probability of $A$ given $B$, written $P(A\mid B)$, is defined to be $\dfrac{P(A\text{ and }B)}{P(B)}$ (assuming $P(B)>0$).

Bayes's Law states that if $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ are both nonzero, then $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(B\mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}$. Prove Bayes's Law using the definition of conditional probability.
dmm-2010-power-01.answer: $P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)P(A)}{P(B)}$ follows from $P(A\text{ and }B)=P(B\mid A)P(A)$.
dmm-2010-power-01.reviewNote: No official answer key was published for the DMM 2010 papers; the answer was worked out independently.

dmm-2010-power-02.prompt:
We denote the probability of event $A$ happening as $P(A)$. The conditional probability of $A$ given $B$, written $P(A\mid B)$, is defined to be $\dfrac{P(A\text{ and }B)}{P(B)}$ (assuming $P(B)>0$).

Show that $P(A\text{ and }B\mid C)=P(B\mid C)\cdot P(A\mid B\text{ and }C)$, assuming that each event or set of events occurs with nonzero probability.
dmm-2010-power-02.answer: $P(A\text{ and }B\mid C)=P(B\mid C)P(A\mid B\text{ and }C)$ by cancelling $P(B\text{ and }C)$.
